summary: At the lunar south pole the Sun grazes the horizon and the Earth hovers only a few degrees above it, so a single distant ridge can decide whether a lander has power and a link to Earth. details:
OVERVIEW

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a browser-based decision-support tool for the rapid assessment of lunar landing sites and dates. For any location on the Moon and any instant between 1969 and 2060 it determines the topocentric positions of the Sun and the Earth relative to the local terrain horizon and derives the quantities that govern surface operations: solar illumination and available power, direct-to-Earth (DTE) line of sight, ground-station coverage, and the time remaining until sunset or Earthset. Several site–date scenarios can be compared side by side, and the effect of a schedule slip can be evaluated over a full year in a fraction of a second.

PROBLEM

At the lunar south pole, the target of most upcoming missions, the Sun never rises more than about 1.5° above the mean horizon and the Earth oscillates within a few degrees of it because of libration. Under these grazing geometries a single ridge tens of kilometres away determines whether a lander has power or communication, and a displacement of one kilometre or a delay of a few days can change mission feasibility. Existing resources (JPL Horizons, QuickMap, Moon Trek) are authoritative but designed for expert analysis; combining ephemerides with terrain for each candidate site and date is slow, and calculations on a smooth sphere are not valid at the poles.

METHOD

Ephemerides. Positions of the Sun and the Earth are computed with the NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE toolkit from the DE440 planetary ephemeris and the high-precision lunar orientation kernel, expressed in the lunar Mean-Earth/Polar-Axis frame used by LOLA products, with light-time and stellar-aberration corrections. They are sampled hourly over 1969–2060 and interpolated in the browser with cubic Lagrange polynomials; site parallax is applied geometrically.

Terrain horizon. For every catalogue site a 360° horizon profile (0.5° azimuth step) is ray-cast through NASA LRO LOLA digital elevation models on a curved Moon: the 20 m/px south-pole model (LDEM_80S_20MPP_ADJ), the 20 m/px north-pole model and the global 237 m/px model, using a multi-resolution march whose range adapts to the maximum possible relief. Horizons for user-defined coordinates are computed in the browser from 240 m/px polar and 8 px/deg global grids. In the absence of an atmosphere no refraction is applied; the horizon is the true terrain skyline including the geometric dip.

Operational metrics. Illumination is quantified as the fraction of the finite solar disc above the terrain profile. Sunrise, sunset, Earthrise and Earthset are located by adaptive scanning and refined by bisection to one second. Power is estimated for Sun-tracking and horizontal arrays from the visible disc fraction, solar elevation and the actual Sun distance. A DTE link requires the Earth to clear the terrain by a configurable mask and the Moon to be above the elevation mask of at least one of 13 deep-space ground stations (NASA DSN and partner agencies).

Landing-window analysis. Candidate landing epochs are scanned against user-defined requirements (solar elevation at landing, duration of continuous sunlight, communication coverage over the surface mission), yielding the feasible windows that remain after a schedule change.

VALIDATION

Computed solar and terrestrial azimuth and elevation agree with the JPL Horizons System to within 0.0002° for seven sites at dates between 1969 and 2040. The in-browser engine reproduces the SPICE reference to 0.0000015°. The solar elevation at the Apollo 11 landing is reproduced as 10.70°, identical to Horizons. The full validation procedure and the known limitations are documented in the repository.

FUNCTIONALITY

Explore: status at a chosen instant with countdowns to the next sunset, sunrise, Earthset and Earthrise; a 360° sky panorama showing the Sun and the Earth at true angular size against the terrain skyline; a mission timeline.

Compare: side-by-side key figures for several scenarios with a transparent scoring scheme and a generated verdict.

Plan: landing-window scan and a year-long illumination and visibility map.

Maps: a 3D globe with the real terminator that zooms out to the Earth at its true size and distance and shows spacecraft currently in lunar orbit (JPL Horizons trajectories); global and polar maps with LOLA average-illumination layers.

Learn: short explanations of lunar lighting and communication driven by live results.

62 catalogued sites (Apollo, Luna, Surveyor, Chang'e, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, commercial landers, Artemis III candidate regions) plus arbitrary coordinates; every value links to its primary data source; scenarios are shareable as links and exportable as CSV or JSON.

BENEFITS AND EXPECTED IMPACT

The tool reduces the evaluation of an alternative site or date from hours of work across several expert systems to seconds, which directly supports re-planning after launch delays and hardware changes. Science and engineering teams can reason from the same quantitative picture. Because it is a static web application that requires no server, installation or account and works offline, it is equally accessible to mission planners, educators, students and the public, and shows with real data why landing at the lunar poles is difficult.

CREATIVITY

The project combines ephemeris computation and high-resolution terrain into a single interactive view that is expressed in operational terms (time to sunset, feasible landing windows) rather than raw angles. The entire computational pipeline, including terrain ray-casting for arbitrary coordinates, runs in the user's browser, and the whole dataset is reproducible from NASA sources with one command-line pipeline.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Absence of atmospheric refraction; lunar curvature and horizon dip; finite angular size of the Sun and the Earth; optical and physical libration; topocentric parallax; light-time and aberration; observer height above the surface; terrain resolution and its effect on horizon accuracy; ground-station elevation masks; leap seconds and time scales. Limitations: lander-scale relief and boulders are not modelled, power figures are geometric (no thermal or electrical model), and communication is evaluated as line of sight without a link budget.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, SciPy, Numba, SpiceyPy, Pillow, tifffile) for the data pipeline and reference implementation; JavaScript (ES modules, no framework or build step), Canvas 2D and three.js for the application; pytest and the Node.js test runner for automated testing; JPL Horizons API for independent validation. Source code: https://github.com/Vladi2lav/nasa-h
